n: The second friend, Bildad, now speaks. He is blunter than Eliphaz and relies on the wisdom of tradition.
He opens impatiently: How long will you go on? Your words are just a blast of hot air.
Bildad’s central question: Does God ever twist justice? Of course not. But he assumes that means Job’s suffering must be deserved.
With painful cruelty, Bildad suggests Job’s children died because they sinned. He turns theology into a weapon against a grieving father.

f.w: cast them away for their transgression
f.g: Literally “gave them into the hand of their transgression.”

n: If you would earnestly seek God and plead with Him...
...and if you are truly pure and upright, God would rouse Himself for you and restore your rightful home. The “if” implies Bildad doubts Job’s innocence.

f.g: He would rise up to act on your behalf.

n: Your beginning would seem small compared to your future greatness. Ironically, this comes true in Job 42 — but not for the reasons Bildad thinks.

f.w: thy latter end should greatly increase

n: Bildad appeals to tradition: ask earlier generations and learn what their fathers discovered.
We were born only yesterday and know nothing; our lives are as fleeting as a shadow.

f.w: our days upon earth are a shadow

n: The ancients will teach you from their deep understanding. Tradition can carry real wisdom — but it can also be misapplied.
Can papyrus grow without a marsh, or reeds without water? Bildad begins a nature lesson.
Cut off from water, such plants wither even while green, faster than other plants.

f.g: Its freshness, still in full growth.

n: So it is with those who forget God: their hope dies. Bildad implies Job is godless.
Their confidence is as fragile as a spider’s web.
He leans on his house, but it collapses; he grabs hold, but it won’t hold. Trusting in anything but God gives way.

f.w: He shall lean upon his house

n: Bildad shifts to a new picture: a well-watered plant thriving in the sun, spreading through the garden.
Its roots wrap around rocks and grip the stones. It seems secure.
But once it is torn out, its place denies ever knowing it. The wicked vanish without a trace.
That’s the “joy” of the wicked — short-lived — and other plants spring up in its place. Bildad’s tone is mocking.

f.g: Said ironically — this is all his “happiness” amounts to.

n: God won’t reject a blameless person or help evildoers. Bildad uses the same word that described Job in chapter 1 — “perfect” — without realizing it fits Job exactly.
He will yet fill your mouth with laughter and your lips with shouts of joy. A hopeful promise, though offered on a condition.
Your enemies will be covered with shame, and the tents of the wicked will disappear. Bildad means well at the end, but his view leaves no room for innocent suffering.
